difficulty_reason: Technically trivial: one short registration form (name, homepage, callback URL) and the client ID/secret are issued immediately.

approval.notes: GitHub's OAuth app documentation contains no review or approval step anywhere in the registration flow; once you click Register application you immediately get a client ID and can generate a client secret.

summary: One of the fastest OAuth setups that exists: a single registration form under Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps, no approval, no verification, no wait. The main judgment call is whether you should build a GitHub App instead - GitHub itself recommends it for most new integrations.

steps.title: Open Developer settings
steps.detail: Click your profile picture on any GitHub page, then Settings, then Developer settings in the left sidebar.

steps.title: Create the OAuth app
steps.detail: Under OAuth apps, click New OAuth App (or Register a new application on first use).

steps.title: Fill the registration form
steps.detail: Application name, Homepage URL, optional description, and Authorization callback URL. Only include information you consider public - GitHub warns against sensitive data such as internal URLs.

steps.title: Decide on device flow and token expiry
steps.detail: Enable Device Flow only if your app will use it. Expire user access tokens is enabled by default; leave it on unless your code cannot yet handle short-lived tokens.

steps.title: Register and copy credentials
steps.detail: Click Register application. You get a client ID immediately and can generate a client secret. Store the secret outside your repo.

requirements: A GitHub account (personal or an organization you administer)
A public homepage URL for your app
At least one authorization callback URL
nuances: GitHub's own docs recommend building a GitHub App instead of an OAuth app for most cases: GitHub Apps get fine-grained permissions, per-repository access, and short-lived tokens.
A user or organization can own at most 100 OAuth apps.
You can register up to 10 callback URLs on one OAuth app.
OAuth apps can only act on behalf of a user; they cannot act independently.

common_blockers.problem: Choosing an OAuth app when the integration really needs GitHub App capabilities (fine-grained repo permissions, acting independently of a user).
common_blockers.solution: Check GitHub's own OAuth Apps vs GitHub Apps comparison before registering - GitHub recommends GitHub Apps for most new integrations, and switching later means re-registering and re-authorizing users.

agent_can_do: Draft the registration values (name, homepage, callback URLs)
Compare OAuth app vs GitHub App for your use case
Prepare the authorization URL and token exchange code
human_must_do: Click through Settings > Developer settings while logged in
Generate and store the client secret

evidence.claim: Registration is a single form (name, homepage URL, optional description, callback URL) under Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps, ending in Register application.
Up to 10 callback URLs are allowed per OAuth app; device flow is optional; expiring user tokens are on by default.
A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.
GitHub recommends considering a GitHub App instead: fine-grained permissions, per-repo access, short-lived tokens, ability to act independently of a user.
The registration page https://github.com/settings/applications/new redirects to login when unauthenticated (HTTP 302) - the console is login-gated, observed 2026-10-20.

uncertainties: GitHub publishes no explicit statement that OAuth apps need no approval; this conclusion comes from the complete absence of any review step in the official registration documentation.
